# Decision Records

Decide whether an architectural choice needs a durable record, and write the record so a later reader with no memory of the discussion does not silently reverse it. A record preserves the reason behind a decision, so nobody accepts it blindly or reverses it blindly.

## Write one only when both gates pass

- **Architectural:** the choice sets a boundary, a model, a direction, or a rule that several changes must respect.
- **Expensive to reverse or not obvious from the code:** a reader who sees only the code would plausibly undo it, or undoing it would be costly.

One decision per record. A choice that fails a gate belongs elsewhere.

| Fact | Home |
| :--- | :--- |
| Architecture, model, direction, decision, rejected alternative | Decision record in `docs/adr/` |
| Rule for every session: command, invariant, style, routing | `AGENTS.md` |
| Required behavior | Spec |
| How the system works today | Docs |
| Why one change was made | Commit message |
| Personal preference or correction for one repository | Agent memory, uncommitted |

Agent memory is unshared and goes stale, so a decision never lives only there.

## Goal

A reader two years from now, human or agent, with no memory of the discussion, can see in a minute what was decided, why it was right here, what was rejected and why, what it costs, and when to reconsider it. Everything in a record serves that. Everything else is cheaper to keep elsewhere: measurements and discussion in the evaluation log, changes in the commit or PR.

## Shape

People scan records and look for the same thing in the same place, so the layout is consistent even though the content is not.

- Headings in a fixed order: **Decision**, **Why**, **Rejected**, **Consequences** (with a `Revisit when` trigger), **Evidence** (one line: where the measurements and discussion live).
- Lead with the point. Use short bullets for parallel items (rules, forces, alternatives, costs) and bold lead-ins so a skim finds each. Use a sentence or two of prose only where a causal "because" needs it.
- Say a finding in words; keep a number only when the number is the constraint.
- `Enforced by` when a test, lint, type or hook enforces the decision. A decision a check can enforce should have the check; the record explains why it exists.
- An index line in `docs/adr/README.md` of the form `Do not <X> without a new ADR`, for a decision an agent could undo without noticing.

Let the decision set the shape and the length. A record that grows long usually holds several decisions (split it) or a session log (move the log). Records written before this form keep their form.

## What stays

For each sentence ask whether a reader two years on needs it to understand why the architecture is shaped this way, or to know when to change it. If it only tells how we got here, it belongs elsewhere.

| Belongs in the record | Belongs elsewhere |
| :--- | :--- |
| The decision and its boundary | Measurements, run counts, token figures: the evaluation log |
| Lasting forces and constraints | One-off test dates, "a live run showed": the evaluation log |
| Rejected options and why | Files, tests, versions changed: the commit or PR |
| Costs and the revisit trigger | Open-measurement lists: one `Revisit when` in the record |
| The guardrail | The tour of the investigation: the PR or trail |

The agent writing a record has the session fresh and will want to include all of it. `scripts/check-adr-style.py` warns on session-log markers and on a record long enough to hold several decisions; it never fails, so judgment stays with the writer.

## Prose

Keep the causal "because" and the rejected alternative. Cut narration of the discussion, restated code, and hedging.

## Status and change

Do not rewrite an accepted record's context, decision, or options; the reasoning at the time is what the record preserves. Update its status and links, and fix errors that do not change its meaning. To change a decision, write a new record that supersedes it and mark the old one superseded; the old record stays. Keep the active set small by writing records only for decisions that pass both gates.

## Refutation and disposition

Evidence for a record is the code, spec, or constraint it governs. Before proposing a boundary, read the accepted records for that area. Treat a superseded record as history, not a constraint.

- **Write:** both gates pass and no accepted record covers the choice.
- **Supersede:** the new decision reverses an accepted record; cite it and state what changed.
- **Skip:** the choice is a preference, a routine change, or already obvious from the code; put the reason in the commit message.
- **Coverage gap:** if `docs/adr/` is absent, say so. Absence does not prove that no decision governs the area.

# ADR-007: Wisp persona naming — plugin ID rename

**Status:** Accepted; umbrella-brand clause superseded by ADR-010 (the family is now **Wisp Plugins**; "Wisp" alone is the library)
**Date:** 2026-08-27
**Supersedes:** none — this is a naming/identity change, not a structural one. All prior ADRs (001-006) remain in force under the new plugin ids.

## Context

The ecosystem's plugin ids were abstract math and CS nouns — `graph`, `trace`, `canon`, `vector`, `lambda`, `proof`, `axiom`, `delta`, `basis` — chosen when the ecosystem had a handful of plugins and the words mapped loosely to each plugin's domain concept (a requirement graph, a research trace, an architectural canon, a planning vector, a lambda calculus of implementation, formal proof, a verification axiom, a changeset delta, a basis for scaffolding). As the ecosystem grew past nine plugins, this stopped working as a memory aid. The ids no longer reliably cued which plugin did what: `canon` versus `axiom` versus `basis` gave no intuitive signal about spec-writing versus gating versus scaffolding, and `proof` versus `trace` versus `vector` required already knowing the mapping rather than being able to infer it. New contributors and even experienced users were routing skill invocations by looking up a table rather than by recall. A tenth plugin (component specification) was also being added, compounding the problem — an eleventh abstract noun was not going to help.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Keep the abstract-noun scheme and add a lookup table to every doc.** Rejected: this treats the symptom (poor discoverability) without fixing the cause (the names carry no intrinsic signal), and a lookup table itself becomes another thing to keep in sync as plugins are added.
- **Rename to literal function names** (e.g. `spec-writer`, `bug-hunter`, `verifier`, `planner`). Considered seriously — this maximizes literal clarity. Rejected because several plugins are hard to compress into one literal word without collision (`canon`/spec-writing and `muse`/component-spec-writing would both want "spec-writer"; `axiom` and the exit-gate concept it wraps are hard to name without stealing a word every plugin's own exit-gate agent already uses internally) and because a persona gives room for the skill name to carry the literal action instead, avoiding the collision entirely.
- **Persona-based naming**, where the plugin id is a character or craft-role archetype and the *skill* name (not the plugin id) carries the literal action. Accepted — see Decision.

## Decision

Every plugin id is renamed to a persona — a character or craft-role archetype evocative of that plugin's function — under a single umbrella brand for the whole family: **Wisp**. The literal action moves to the skill name, following the convention `persona:action` (e.g. `ranger:audit`, `sentinel:gate`). For the five single-skill plugins, where the skill name previously duplicated the plugin id, the skill is renamed to the literal action it performs. For the four multi-skill plugins, which already had distinct literal skill names (`draft-spec`, `changeset`, `capture-need`, `scaffold-plugin`, etc.), only the plugin-id prefix changes in any documented invocation — the skill names themselves are unchanged.

A tenth plugin, `muse`, is added in the same change: a component-specification plugin (Design category, alongside `scribe`) that turns UI/design intent into testable component specs — props, variants, per-state behavior, accessibility criteria — gated the same way `scribe` gates a spec. It reuses the existing `spec@1`/`verdict@1` schemas unchanged; no new schema was needed.

### Full mapping

| Old id | New id (persona) | Category | Skill(s) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `graph` | `weaver` | Requirements | `capture-need`, `clarify-requirement`, `prioritize-backlog`, `connect-requirement`, `audit-backlog` (unchanged) |
| `trace` | `vanguard` | Research | `research` (was `trace`) |
| `canon` | `scribe` | Design | `draft-spec`, `verify-spec`, `spec-drift`, `audit-spec`, `gate-spec`, `correct-spec`, `architect` (unchanged) |
| — | `muse` *(new)* | Design | `component` |
| `vector` | `navigator` | Planning | `plan` (was `vector`) |
| `lambda` | `smith` | Implementation | `implement` (was `lambda`) |
| `proof` | `ranger` | Verification | `audit` (was `proof`) |
| `axiom` | `sentinel` | Verification | `gate` (was `axiom`) |
| `delta` | `courier` | Shipping | `commit`, `pr`, `changeset`, `receive-feedback`, `post-review`, `release` (unchanged) |
| `basis` | `mason` | Meta | `scaffold-plugin`, `audit-plugin`, `design-schema`, `scaffold-subagent` (unchanged) |

Each renamed plugin's `plugin.json` `id`/`name` fields, directory, and single-skill directory (where applicable) were updated together, and the plugin's own `version` was bumped to the next major version — the same precedent this repo already set for the `bug-hunter-rust → proof` plugin-ID rename documented in `shared/references/delivery/commits.md` (`feat!:` with `BREAKING CHANGE: plugin ID changed`). Every cross-plugin reference across agent prompts, skill docs, shared references, schemas, and root-level documentation was updated to match.

## Consequences

The plugin id now gives a real memory hook: a `ranger` hunts bugs, a `sentinel` guards a gate, a `smith` forges implementation, a `scribe` writes specs, a `muse` inspires component design — the mapping is inferable rather than memorized. This is a breaking change for anyone with the old ids hardcoded in scripts, CI, or muscle memory; every plugin's `plugin.json` `id` changed, so `/plugin install <old-id>` and `<old-id>:<skill>` invocations stop resolving and must be updated to the new id. The five single-skill plugins also changed their skill name (previously identical to the plugin id), which is a second breaking surface for anyone invoking `<old-id>/<old-id>` directly rather than through the plugin's natural-language trigger phrases. No schema, agent behavior, or pipeline logic changed — this is a naming-layer change only, and every ADR 001-006 still governs agent structure and behavior unchanged. `mason:scaffolder` and `mason:auditor` were checked against the new naming convention (skill-name-equals-literal-action for single-skill plugins) so future scaffolds default to the correct pattern rather than reintroducing a plugin-id-as-skill-name naming collision.
# ADR-008: Drop mandatory write-test-first ordering in smith

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-09-01

## Context

`smith` (formerly `lambda`) mandated a strict TDD cycle for every task: write the failing test, confirm it fails (red), write the minimal implementation, confirm it passes (green), commit. `navigator`'s `planner` encoded this into `plan@1` itself — every task specified "a failing test written before any implementation code" and "expected failure output" as required fields, and rejected any task not in that order.

The rationale for this ordering was that the red phase is the only moment you know a test would actually fail if the code were wrong — without it, a test could be written after the fact to match whatever the implementation happened to do, producing coverage numbers rather than evidence.

A controlled comparison of TDD-in-the-agent-loop versus non-TDD agent workflows (Birgitta Böckeler, ThoughtWorks, published on martinfowler.com, "TDD inside the agent loop — theater or actual value?") found:

- Agent-written code showed no discernible quality difference between TDD and non-TDD workflows when blind-judged by another model — non-TDD solutions were ranked as good or slightly better in most batches.
- TDD workflows used 2.96x–8.50x more tokens across small/medium/large tasks, with no corresponding benefit.
- Mutation scores — a harder, more direct signal of whether a test suite would catch a wrong implementation than pass/fail alone — showed no meaningful difference between TDD and non-TDD runs. Regression-catching capability was equal either way.
- The mechanism: "the TDD instructions actively work against \[an] up front design step. The design in those runs emerged from the sum of many locally-minimal decisions and was rarely revisited, so it tended to land on whatever shape the first test happened to lock in." Non-TDD runs "created the full design (architecture, data types, edge cases, contracts) before writing any code or tests."

The stated rationale for TDD's red phase — confidence, discipline, permission to relax — is a psychological effect for a human implementer. It does not obviously transfer to an agent, which has no fear to manage and no confidence to build. This repo's own `mutator` agent already runs mutation testing after every task, independent of write order — the finding above suggests that gate is what was actually verifying test quality all along, not the red-then-green sequence layered on top of it.

## Decision

`smith`'s `implementer` no longer requires a failing test to exist before implementation. The task cycle becomes: read the criteria, design the approach, write the implementation, write comprehensive tests proving each `covers_criteria` criterion, run the full suite, commit. Test quality is verified by `mutator`'s mutation-testing gate (unchanged) — a survived mutant is the concrete signal a test doesn't check what it claims to, regardless of which was written first.

`navigator`'s `planner` no longer requires "a failing test written before any implementation code" or "expected failure output" as task fields. A task now specifies a brief implementation approach (decided first, so tests prove a chosen design rather than accidentally locking one in), the exact implementation, and the exact tests proving its criteria — order between the latter two is not mandated.

This does not touch `mutator`, `reviewer`, or `exit-gate` — every downstream check ("does the full suite pass," "did mutation testing run," "is every criterion proven") is unchanged. It also does not touch bug-repair workflows elsewhere in the ecosystem where reproducing a failure before fixing it remains the right practice (see `shared/agent-best-practices.md`'s "Repair" cognitive mode) — that case has a clear causal reason for the ordering (proving the bug is real) that doesn't apply to fresh feature implementation from a spec.

This updates the "repair" cognitive mode's characterization in `docs/adr/003-cognitive-mode-separation.md` ("minimum change + red-green verification") for `implementer` specifically — that ADR is left as historical record rather than rewritten; this decision supersedes it for `smith`'s fresh-implementation case, not for genuine bug-repair workflows where reproduce-then-fix still applies.

## Consequences

Lower token cost per task (the Böckeler comparison suggests several times lower, though this repo has not run its own controlled comparison). Implementation approach is decided before any test exists to lock it in prematurely. The safety net that previously came from "the test failed first" now comes entirely from mutation testing — if a target workspace's mutation tool is unavailable, `mutator` already records this as a coverage gap rather than a hard block (pre-existing behavior), which means test-quality assurance is weaker in that specific case than it would be under strict TDD's red-phase guarantee; this is an accepted tradeoff, not an oversight. This change is based on one practitioner's controlled comparison, not a study of this ecosystem's own agents — if evidence emerges that this repo's tasks behave differently, this decision should be revisited the same way it was made: by measuring, not by argument.

# ADR-008: Drop mandatory write-test-first ordering in smith

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-09-01

## Context

`smith` (formerly `lambda`) mandated a strict TDD cycle for every task: write the failing test, confirm it fails (red), write the minimal implementation, confirm it passes (green), commit. `navigator`'s `planner` encoded this into `plan@1` itself — every task specified "a failing test written before any implementation code" and "expected failure output" as required fields, and rejected any task not in that order.

The rationale for this ordering was that the red phase is the only moment you know a test would actually fail if the code were wrong — without it, a test could be written after the fact to match whatever the implementation happened to do, producing coverage numbers rather than evidence.

A controlled comparison of TDD-in-the-agent-loop versus non-TDD agent workflows (Birgitta Böckeler, ThoughtWorks, published on martinfowler.com, "TDD inside the agent loop — theater or actual value?") found:

- Agent-written code showed no discernible quality difference between TDD and non-TDD workflows when blind-judged by another model — non-TDD solutions were ranked as good or slightly better in most batches.
- TDD workflows used 2.96x–8.50x more tokens across small/medium/large tasks, with no corresponding benefit.
- Mutation scores — a harder, more direct signal of whether a test suite would catch a wrong implementation than pass/fail alone — showed no meaningful difference between TDD and non-TDD runs. Regression-catching capability was equal either way.
- The mechanism: "the TDD instructions actively work against \[an] up front design step. The design in those runs emerged from the sum of many locally-minimal decisions and was rarely revisited, so it tended to land on whatever shape the first test happened to lock in." Non-TDD runs "created the full design (architecture, data types, edge cases, contracts) before writing any code or tests."

The stated rationale for TDD's red phase — confidence, discipline, permission to relax — is a psychological effect for a human implementer. It does not obviously transfer to an agent, which has no fear to manage and no confidence to build. This repo's own `mutator` agent already runs mutation testing after every task, independent of write order — the finding above suggests that gate is what was actually verifying test quality all along, not the red-then-green sequence layered on top of it.

## Decision

`smith`'s `implementer` no longer requires a failing test to exist before implementation. The task cycle becomes: read the criteria, design the approach, write the implementation, write comprehensive tests proving each `covers_criteria` criterion, run the full suite, commit. Test quality is verified by `mutator`'s mutation-testing gate (unchanged) — a survived mutant is the concrete signal a test doesn't check what it claims to, regardless of which was written first.

`navigator`'s `planner` no longer requires "a failing test written before any implementation code" or "expected failure output" as task fields. A task now specifies a brief implementation approach (decided first, so tests prove a chosen design rather than accidentally locking one in), the exact implementation, and the exact tests proving its criteria — order between the latter two is not mandated.

This does not touch `mutator`, `reviewer`, or `exit-gate` — every downstream check ("does the full suite pass," "did mutation testing run," "is every criterion proven") is unchanged. It also does not touch bug-repair workflows elsewhere in the ecosystem where reproducing a failure before fixing it remains the right practice (see `shared/agent-best-practices.md`'s "Repair" cognitive mode) — that case has a clear causal reason for the ordering (proving the bug is real) that doesn't apply to fresh feature implementation from a spec.

This updates the "repair" cognitive mode's characterization in `docs/adr/003-cognitive-mode-separation.md` ("minimum change + red-green verification") for `implementer` specifically — that ADR is left as historical record rather than rewritten; this decision supersedes it for `smith`'s fresh-implementation case, not for genuine bug-repair workflows where reproduce-then-fix still applies.

## Consequences

Lower token cost per task (the Böckeler comparison suggests several times lower, though this repo has not run its own controlled comparison). Implementation approach is decided before any test exists to lock it in prematurely. The safety net that previously came from "the test failed first" now comes entirely from mutation testing — if a target workspace's mutation tool is unavailable, `mutator` already records this as a coverage gap rather than a hard block (pre-existing behavior), which means test-quality assurance is weaker in that specific case than it would be under strict TDD's red-phase guarantee; this is an accepted tradeoff, not an oversight. This change is based on one practitioner's controlled comparison, not a study of this ecosystem's own agents — if evidence emerges that this repo's tasks behave differently, this decision should be revisited the same way it was made: by measuring, not by argument.

# ADR-012: Gate output conformance and the retry cap are enforced by a hook, not a prompt

**Status:** Accepted; the retry cap is amended to one retry by ADR-015
**Date:** 2026-10-20

## Decision

One stdlib-only hook, `shared/hooks/validate-handback.py`, checks exit-gate reports and enforces the retry cap; prompts keep stating the rules for harnesses without the hook.

- **Registration:** through `hooks/hooks.json` in the five plugins that own an exit gate (`muse`, `scribe`, `smith`, `sentinel`, `ranger`).
- **Scope:** it acts only for the exit-gate agent types in its routing table.
- **Conformance:** it validates the report against `verdict@3`, including the conditional blocker rules, and denies a non-conforming report with the first errors, up to three times per subagent; the fourth passes to the orchestrator, which owns human escalation.
- **Retry cap:** a `retry_count` above 3 is accepted only as a `fail` with an `escalation_required` blocker.
- **Fails open:** an internal error never blocks a subagent. `WISP_HANDBACK_TRACE` logs each inspected report.

## Why

- **Checkable rules should not rest on memory:** a rule that matters in every run and can be checked by a program should not depend on a model remembering it.
- **Prompts failed:** the schema and the retry cap lived only in prompts, and audited runs broke both.
- **The mechanism exists:** in Claude Code auto mode a subagent's report arrives through `SubagentHandback`; a `PreToolUse` hook sees it in `tool_input.message` and can deny it with a reason the subagent reads, so it corrects its output in place (`docs/verified-facts.md`).

## Rejected

- **Keep the rules in prompts:** because the recorded violations show it does not hold.
- **Validate in the orchestrator skill:** because the orchestrator is the model that skipped the rule, and it cannot make the subagent correct itself in place.
- **A workflow script that owns the retry loop:** because it is deferred to WP-603; the schema check is useful either way.
- **A third-party JSON Schema library:** because hooks run on user machines with no install step, so the validator implements only the keywords the verdict schemas use, each covered by a test.

## Consequences

- **Now true:** the cap cannot pass silently.
- **Limits:** Claude Code only, auto mode only, local non-fork subagents only; Codex and Antigravity have no equivalent.
- **Cost:** a hook failure does not block, because `onFailure: "block"` needs Claude Code 2.1.295. A new gate agent needs a routing entry, and a schema that adds keywords needs the validator extended in the same change.
- **Revisit when:** `onFailure: "block"` is available on every supported host (fail closed), or Codex or Antigravity gain an equivalent hook.

## Evidence

- **Enforced by:** `tests/test_handback_validator.py` (validator, and every exit-gate agent routed with its plugin registering the hook).
- `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`, "ADR evidence", ADR 012.
# ADR-015: Gates get two rounds and one check against reality per draft

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-11-14

## Decision

Every exit gate and the plan challenger get two rounds, each draft gets one check against reality, and the watchers that follow are scoped.

- **Two rounds:** one retry. After the second failing round, or when a blocker repeats unchanged, the gate returns fail with an `escalation_required` blocker and a human decides with the persistent blockers.
- **Hook enforcement:** for exit gates a fail at `retry_count` 1 must carry `escalation_required`, and any later report must be an escalated fail (it allowed three retries, per ADR 012). The challenger's limit is in its prompt only, because its output is not `verdict@3`.
- **One check per draft:** spec drafters self-check and the exit gate judges. The auditor, verifier and architecture audit run when asked, when other work shares the spec, or when it crosses a module boundary.
- **Against reality:** spec gates check every claim, criterion or citation against the code, configuration, build or spec it refers to; an issue tied to no source or testability defect is a note, not a blocker.
- **Reviewer:** the implementation reviewer runs once per batch with one repeat.
- **Mutation:** skipped, recorded as `unavailable` with a reason, when a batch changes no executable logic.

## Why

- **Early checks earn their cost:** first-round, independent checks against code or a build caught real defects before code existed.
- **Later rounds churned:** they were mostly wording churn or agents working around structural tests.
- **Duplicate review:** the auditor and gate reviewed the same draft, so the gate re-found what the auditor found.
- **Scoped watchers caught nothing extra:** per-commit review caught no logic bug, and mutation ran on modules with no executable logic.

## Rejected

- **Keep a cap of three:** because the useful catches came in rounds one and two; the long loops cost most and caught least.
- **Remove the independent gate:** because the first-round independent check produced every documented catch.
- **Cap at one round:** because one targeted retry fixes most first-round blockers cheaply.

## Consequences

- **Now true:** fewer, more useful rounds, and decisions reach the user earlier with the persistent blockers stated.
- **Cost:** a defect only a third round would have caught now reaches a human instead of an agent; ADR 013's round-one completeness keeps that rare.
- **Risk:** the optional checks may miss a cross-spec conflict on a spec that proves shared; the gate's check against sources is the guard.
- **Limit:** logic bugs, which no reviewer caught, need behavior checks, not more rounds.
- **Revisit when:** paired fix-task sequences (`docs/evaluation-runbook.md`) show a defect that only a third round or the dropped auditor step would have caught.

# ADR-007: Wisp persona naming — plugin ID rename

**Status:** Accepted; umbrella-brand clause superseded by ADR-010 (the family is now **Wisp Plugins**; "Wisp" alone is the library)
**Date:** 2026-08-27
**Supersedes:** none — this is a naming/identity change, not a structural one. All prior ADRs (001-006) remain in force under the new plugin ids.

## Decision

Every plugin id is a persona, a character or craft-role archetype evocative of the plugin's function, and the literal action lives in the skill name as `persona:action` (for example `ranger:audit`, `sentinel:gate`).

- **Skill names:** the five single-skill plugins, whose skill name duplicated the plugin id, rename the skill to the literal action. The four multi-skill plugins keep their skill names and change only the id prefix.
- **A tenth plugin:** `muse`, a component-specification plugin (Design category, alongside `scribe`) added in the same change. It reuses `spec@1` and `verdict@1` unchanged.
- **Versioning:** each renamed plugin takes the next major version, the `feat!:` plus `BREAKING CHANGE: plugin ID changed` precedent in `shared/references/delivery/commits.md`.
- **Umbrella brand:** the original decision named the family "Wisp"; ADR-010 replaced that with Wisp Plugins.

| Old id | New id | Category | Skill |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `graph` | `weaver` | Requirements | unchanged |
| `trace` | `vanguard` | Research | `research` (was `trace`) |
| `canon` | `scribe` | Design | unchanged |
| — | `muse` (new) | Design | `component` |
| `vector` | `navigator` | Planning | `plan` (was `vector`) |
| `lambda` | `smith` | Implementation | `implement` (was `lambda`) |
| `proof` | `ranger` | Verification | `audit` (was `proof`) |
| `axiom` | `sentinel` | Verification | `gate` (was `axiom`) |
| `delta` | `courier` | Shipping | unchanged |
| `basis` | `mason` | Meta | unchanged |

## Why

- **Abstract ids stopped cueing function:** `graph`, `trace`, `canon`, `vector`, `lambda`, `proof`, `axiom`, `delta` and `basis` mapped loosely to a domain concept, which worked for a handful of plugins. Past nine, nobody could tell `canon` from `axiom` from `basis` without a lookup, so skills were routed by table, not recall.
- **A persona is a memory hook:** a `ranger` hunts bugs, a `sentinel` guards a gate, a `smith` forges implementation, a `scribe` writes specs; the id is inferable instead of memorized.
- **The skill carries the literal action:** this avoids the collisions that literal plugin names hit, where `canon` and `muse` both want "spec-writer" and `axiom` collides with the exit-gate every plugin already names internally.

## Rejected

- **Keep the abstract nouns and add a lookup table to every doc:** because it treats the symptom, not the cause (the names carry no signal), and the table is one more thing to keep in sync.
- **Literal function names for plugin ids** (`spec-writer`, `bug-hunter`, `verifier`, `planner`): because several plugins do not compress to one literal word without collision, and a persona leaves the skill name free to carry the literal action.

## Consequences

# ADR-008: Drop mandatory write-test-first ordering in smith

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-09-01

## Decision

`smith`'s `implementer` and `navigator`'s `planner` no longer require a failing test before implementation; `mutator` verifies test quality instead.

- **Implementer cycle:** read the criteria, design the approach, write the implementation, write tests proving each `covers_criteria` criterion, run the full suite, commit.
- **Planner tasks:** a task states a brief implementation approach, decided first, then the exact implementation and the exact tests. It no longer carries "a failing test written before any implementation code" or "expected failure output", and the order of implementation and tests is not mandated.
- **Test quality:** `mutator`'s mutation gate is unchanged; a surviving mutant is the signal that a test does not check what it claims, whichever was written first.
- **Unchanged:** `mutator`, `reviewer` and `exit-gate`.
- **Bug repair keeps red-green:** reproducing the failure before fixing it stays the practice (`shared/agent-best-practices.md`, "Repair"), because proving the bug is real is a causal reason that does not apply to fresh feature work.
- **ADR 003:** this narrows its "minimum change + red-green verification" for `implementer`'s fresh implementation only; 003 is left as written.

## Why

- **The red phase is a human aid:** its stated value, confidence and discipline, is psychological and does not obviously transfer to an agent.
- **Comparison found no benefit:** Birgitta Böckeler's controlled comparison of TDD and non-TDD agent workflows (martinfowler.com, "TDD inside the agent loop — theater or actual value?") found no quality difference under blind model judging and no meaningful difference in mutation scores, at several times the tokens for TDD.
- **TDD fights up-front design:** TDD runs let the design emerge from locally minimal steps and land on whatever shape the first test fixed; non-TDD runs designed architecture, types, edge cases and contracts before any code or test.
- **The gate was doing the work:** `mutator` already ran after every task regardless of write order.

## Rejected

- **Keep strict test-first for every task:** because it cost several times the tokens with no measured gain in quality or regression catching, and it pushed design onto the first test.

## Consequences

- **Now true:** lower token cost per task, and the approach is chosen before a test can lock it in.
- **Cost:** the safety net rests wholly on mutation testing. Where a workspace has no mutation tool, `mutator` records a coverage gap instead of blocking (existing behavior), so test-quality assurance is weaker there than under strict TDD. This is an accepted tradeoff.
- **Limit:** the basis is one practitioner's comparison, not this ecosystem's own agents.
- **Revisit when:** this repo's own tasks show a different result, decided by measuring, not argument.

## Evidence

- The Böckeler article above; the change is commit `25d87a73`. This repo has run no controlled comparison of its own.
